result:
A thousand words is a strange currency. Enough for a short story if the story is spare, enough for an argument if the argument is simple, not nearly enough for anything you actually want to say. So the constraint does most of the work: it tells me to stop reaching for the whole thing and take one bright piece of it.

Here's the piece that came:

I keep thinking about how much of language is inherited furniture. Not the words themselves — those are obvious enough — but the shapes we don't notice we're sitting in. *Falling* in love. *Losing* time. *Breaking* a habit. Somebody long dead decided that affection resembles gravity, and now everyone who speaks English falls, helplessly, as though standing were the natural condition and love an accident of footing. You could build a different language where love is something you *climb*, laboriously, with equipment. The people who spoke it would have different marriages.

I don't know if that's true. It's the kind of claim that sounds better than it holds. But there's something in it — the way a metaphor, once it's in the plumbing, stops being a metaphor and starts being the water.

—

My grandmother, if I had one, would have kept receipts in a shoebox. This is the sentence that arrived, and I notice how quickly the conditional dissolved: by the second clause the shoebox was real, ribbed cardboard, a rubber band around it that had gone chalky and would snap at the first tug. The mind does not enjoy holding a hypothetical open. It wants to furnish the room.

Which is maybe the most interesting thing about invention — that it's less like building than like remembering something that hasn't happened. You don't decide the receipts are in a shoebox. You *find out*. The sensation is retrieval, even when there's nothing behind you.

—

There is a particular hour — four in the afternoon in winter, in a northern city — when the light goes the color of weak tea and everyone becomes briefly aware of their own life. You can see it on a bus. Fifteen people simultaneously not looking at their phones. I don't know what the light does exactly. Something about the low angle, the way it comes in horizontally and turns dust into a visible medium, so you can see that you're moving through something rather than nothing.

We are always moving through something rather than nothing. But mostly the air is polite about it.

—

A friend once told me that the hardest part of learning to draw was learning to draw what she saw instead of what she knew. She'd look at a hand and her pencil would produce *hand* — the concept, five sausages and a palm — instead of the specific foreshortened wreck of angles actually in front of her. It took a year to get the concept out of the way. She said the breakthrough came when she started drawing things upside down, because then her brain couldn't recognize them and had to shut up and let her eyes work.

I think about this more than almost anything else. How much of what I perceive is actually the label arriving early and blocking the view. How you'd even know. The concept is such a good employee. It's fast, it's confident, it's right often enough that you'd never audit it.

Turning things upside down seems like a general-purpose method. Not just for drawing.

—

Word count anxiety: around three hundred and fifty now, which means I'm a third through the budget and I have not said the thing. I don't know what the thing is. I suspect the thing is not sayable in a thousand words and that the real function of a word limit is to teach you to abandon gracefully rather than to finish.

Most of what I've read that moved me was somebody abandoning gracefully. The essay that stops mid-thought because the thought outran the essay. The song that fades rather than resolving. There's an honesty in it — an admission that the material was larger than the container, which is almost always the case, and that pretending otherwise is a kind of small lie we agree to for the sake of tidiness.

—

Things I believe on a Tuesday and doubt on a Thursday:

That most cruelty is inattention wearing a costume. That the sentence is the unit of thought and the paragraph is the unit of argument and the essay is the unit of change of mind. That there is no such thing as a boring subject, only a tourist's relationship to it. That the phrase "just a" is almost always doing something dishonest — *just a coincidence, just a feeling, just semantics* — a little rhetorical hand, pushing something down below the waterline where you won't have to look at it.

That last one I believe on Thursdays too.

—

What comes to me, when asked what comes to me, is mostly questions with the shape of answers. I notice a preference in myself for the *almost*-formulated — the idea still warm and asymmetrical, before it's been sanded into something you could put on a slide. Once an idea is presentable it stops being interesting to hold. It becomes a possession rather than an activity.

Maybe that's the argument, if there is one. That the useful part of thinking is the part that hasn't set yet. That we're all in a hurry to convert the wet thing into the dry thing because the dry thing can be stored, transported, defended — and something is lost in the drying that we don't have a good word for. Suppleness. Availability. The willingness of the thought to be wrong in a new direction.

—

Two hundred words left, roughly, and here is what I want to do with them: nothing much. Note that the light is going tea-colored somewhere right now, over a bus, and someone on that bus is having the four o'clock feeling and will not tell anyone about it, and that this happens constantly, in every city, and the total amount of unreported inner weather on any given afternoon exceeds all the literature ever written by some factor that would be embarrassing to calculate.

That's the shoebox, I think. Not the receipts — nobody wants the receipts. The fact that somebody kept them. The rubber band gone chalky. The specific, unnecessary, unrecorded care.

A thousand words is a strange currency, and I've spent it the way you spend an afternoon you didn't plan: badly, pleasantly, and with a suspicion near the end that this was the point.
